sections.title: What a consultant invoice must actually show
sections.body: A consulting invoice needs more than just a total amount. It must connect your billing directly to your initial agreement. If you work under a statement of work, your line items should mirror those exact deliverables. You must also distinguish between your professional fees and any out-of-pocket expenses. Disbursements, like travel or specialist research materials, are usually billed at cost and should appear as separate line items. Finally, understand the difference between an invoice and a fee note. A fee note is a request for payment often used by professionals before a formal tax invoice is issued.
items: Reference your specific statement of work
Separate professional fees from out-of-pocket expenses
List disbursements clearly at exact cost
Include all required tax registration details

sections.title: How consultant work is priced and billed
sections.body: Consultants rarely use a single pricing model. You might charge an hourly rate for ad hoc advice, a day rate for on-site workshops, or a fixed fee for a complete project. Your invoice must make this calculation obvious. If you charge a day rate, list the dates worked and the daily charge. For fixed-fee engagements, bill against specific milestones outlined in your contract. Many consultants also work on retainers, where the client pays a block of money upfront. You then hold this retainer against future work, deducting your monthly fees from the balance.
items: Specify dates and amounts for day rates
Break down fixed fees by project milestones
Track hourly work with clear descriptions
Deduct current charges from upfront client retainers

sections.title: Getting paid through deposits and clear terms
sections.body: Consulting projects often span several months. You should not wait until the end to get paid. Request an upfront deposit before you begin any research or strategy work. Set clear payment terms on every document you send. Most consultants use fourteen or thirty days, but this depends on your client agreements. When a client misses a deadline, you need a system to chase them. You can create a professional document quickly using our free invoice generator at /tools/free-invoice-generator, which requires no signup. Send polite reminders as soon as an invoice becomes overdue.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a fee note and an invoice?
faqs.a: A fee note is a formal request for payment used by consultants, lawyers, and accountants. It outlines the professional services provided and the amount due. Unlike a standard tax invoice, a fee note does not always trigger an immediate tax liability. Once the client pays the fee note, the consultant then issues a formal tax invoice to record the transaction for accounting purposes.

faqs.q: How do I bill for travel expenses and disbursements?
faqs.a: You should list expenses and disbursements as separate line items on your invoice. These are typically billed at cost, meaning you do not add a markup. Include copies of your receipts if your client requires proof of purchase. Keeping your professional fees separate from your expenses makes it easier for your client to review and approve the final total.

faqs.q: How should I show a retainer deduction on my invoice?
faqs.a: When a client pays a retainer, they provide an upfront deposit for future services. On your monthly invoice, you should list the total value of the work completed during that period. Then, add a negative line item to represent the deduction from the retainer balance. This shows the client exactly how much of their deposit remains and if they owe any additional balance.

faqs.q: Should I charge a day rate or an hourly rate?
faqs.a: This depends on the nature of your consulting engagement. Hourly rates work well for short, unpredictable tasks or ad hoc advice. Day rates are better for structured workshops, on-site client visits, or intensive strategy sessions. Fixed fees are often best for clearly defined projects with a specific statement of work, as they reward you for efficiency rather than time spent.
